paper_title: Toward Sensory Homeostasis in Autism: Comparative Evaluation of a Recurrent Signal-to-Memory Hierarchy
paper_abstract: Background/Objectives: The signal-to-memory (S2M) hierarchy links Ca²⁺-signal construction and decoding to transcriptional and chromatin changes that may modify subsequent neuronal responsiveness and support sensory homeostasis: adaptation to familiar input while preserving sensitivity to meaningful change. We assessed evidence for its involvement in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) pathogenesis and implications for therapeutic target validation. Methods: The prespecified S2M-44 core was compared with 11 monogenic ASD mouse models, an ASD protein-association network, and 106 schizophrenia-prioritized genes. Exact overlap, molecular association, and functional correspondence were distinguished; broader ASD-gene context and four extension candidates were evaluated separately. Results: Four mouse-model genes matched the core, all transcriptional or chromatin regulators. The protein network represented 27 core proteins, including both IP₃ receptors, ITPR1 and ITPR3, recovered as interactors. Separately reported KDM6B and SETD5 studies demonstrated rescue of downstream neuronal defects, with selected behavioral rescue in the SETD5 model. The schizophrenia set shared one core gene and implicated related signaling operations. Conclusions: These findings strengthen the case for pathogenic involvement of connected S2M operations and prioritize IP₃R-mediated Ca²⁺ release for molecular target validation. Demonstrating target-dependent restoration of signaling and adaptive responsiveness across genetically distinct models would establish a mechanistic foundation for drug discovery.

paper_title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Behaviour for Temporally Structured Crime-Count Prediction
paper_abstract: Predicting crime counts is a difficult technology problem because the data are temporally dependent, uneven across locations and categories, vulnerable to leakage, and often dominated by persistence from prior periods. This study evaluates how distinct machine-learning (ML) regression families behave when applied to temporally structured crime-count data and asks whether increased model complexity produces measurable improvements over a simple seasonal benchmark. This study evaluates five ML regression families - Random Forest Model (RFM), Extreme Gradient Boosting Regressor (XGBR), K-Nearest Neighbor Regressor (KNNR), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Multi-Layer Perceptron Regressor (MLPR) - compared across alternative categorical encoding scenarios (S), while Seasonal Naïve (SNa-ïve) prediction was retained as a transparent benchmark. The experimental protocol used rolling-origin tuning over 2019–2023, a separate 2024 validation period, and a one-pass 2025 held-out comparative evaluation of frozen candidate configurations. The 2025 observations were not used to define features, preprocessing rules, encoding scenarios, hyperparameter grids, or tuned hyperparameters. Because the trained configuration used for the later forecasting demonstration was chosen after inspection of the 2025 comparison, the 2025 scores are treated as comparative evidence across pre-specified candidates rather than as an independent post-selection validation of that forecasting choice. SNaïve achieved the lowest 2025 error (RMSE=44.162; MAE=21.224; R²=0.9669). Among the trained candidates, XGBR S4 had the lowest RMSE (56.449), followed closely by RFM S4 (57.088). Encoding choice affected trained-model behaviour, prediction intervals showed mild undercoverage, local error varied substantially, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis showed that the one-year same-quarter lag was the dominant explanatory feature. The 2026–2027 values are unvalidated model projections and are not findings about future crime outcomes. The paper therefore reports a bounded empirical comparison and reproducible temporal evaluation protocol for this administrative crime-count dataset; it does not claim universal crime prediction, hotspot detection, or a general operational decision rule.

paper_title: Comparative Clinical and Immunological Evaluation of Bulbar Conjunctival Pedicle Grafting and Allogeneic Canine Amniotic Membrane Grafting for the Management of Corneal Ulcers in Dogs
paper_abstract: Background: The cornea is a transparent, avascular, and highly specialized structure that serves as the eye’s primary refractive surface, making it essential for normal vision. Corneal ulcers, commonly resulting from trauma or infection, are a leading cause of ocular morbidity and blindness in dogs. Surgical intervention is often required for deep or non-healing ulcers. Conjunctival grafts help restore corneal integrity but may prolong recovery. Canine amniotic membrane (AM) possesses an-ti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and epithelialization-promoting properties that may enhance corneal wound healing. Methods: Twelve clinical canine cases with corneal ulcers were randomly allocated into two Groups (n = 6 each). Group A underwent bulbar conjunctival pedicle grafting, while Group B received canine amniotic membrane grafts prepared from placentas collected during elective cae-sarean sections. The amniotic membrane was applied in three layers and stabilized with a third-eyelid flap and partial tarsorrhaphy. Postoperative assessment included physiological pa-rameters, detailed ophthalmic examinations, tear production tests, fluorescein dye uptake, and rel-evant biochemical analyses. Results: Complete healing was achieved in five of six dogs in Group A and in all six dogs in Group B. Physiological and biochemical values did not differ significantly between Groups; however, Group B exhibited more rapid epithelialization, reduced postoperative complications, and overall better clinical recovery. Conclusion: Both surgical approaches were effec-tive in managing canine corneal ulcers, but the canine amniotic membrane graft provided superior healing, faster epithelial restoration, and improved clinical outcomes.

paper_title: Rapid Evaluation of Chaboche–Voce Material Model Parameters Through a Fully Reversed Strain-Controlled Test
paper_abstract: Modeling cyclic plasticity remains challenging due to the high computational cost of nonlinear constitutive models and the large number of parameters requiring evaluation, which are often temperature-dependent. This work presents a systematic procedure for identifying the parameters of the Chaboche–Voce model, one of the most widely adopted constitutive models for cyclic plasticity and commonly implemented in finite element software. Due to its nonlinear formulation, however, parameter evaluation is not straightforward. The parameters governing the kinematic hardening response are determined through a simple least-squares fit, yielding an analytical expression for a branch of the mid-life stabilized cycle. The Voce parameters are subsequently obtained by solving an analytical equation followed by a further least-squares fit. The resulting methodology provides a systematic approach for characterizing materials exhibiting both cyclic hardening and softening. The procedure was applied to two materials: 42CrMo4+QT tested at room temperature at different strain ranges for two different values of mean strain and 1Cr-1Mo-0.25V steel tested at different temperatures and strain ranges. The proposed approach provides satisfactory constitutive parameters while requiring virtually negligible computational cost, making it suitable for efficient material characterization and subsequent finite element implementation.

paper_title: AI in Education from CAI to AGI: A Narrative Review and Conceptual Framework
paper_abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping education, yet research remains fragmented across technological streams and often conflates technical capability with demonstrated educational effectiveness. This narrative review synthesizes representative literature published mainly between 2010 and 2026 to trace the evolution of AI-enabled education from computer-assisted instruction toward adaptive, immersive, generative, and potentially more general forms of intelligence. It compares three major technological streams: intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems, extended reality (XR), and large language model-based generative AI. The review finds that intelligent tutoring systems support learner modeling, adaptive feedback, and personalization, but their evidence base is methodologically heterogeneous. XR shows comparatively more consolidated evidence, particularly through systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with generally positive but context-dependent effects on engagement and learning outcomes. Generative AI expands dialogic explanation, scaffolding, content generation, and personalized support, although learner-outcome evidence remains limited relative to capability benchmarking. Building on these findings, the review proposes a Technology–Mechanism–Outcome–Challenge framework and argues that future progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI) should be evaluated through learning mechanisms, measurable outcomes, human oversight, equity, and responsible governance.

paper_title: Cross-Dataset Evaluation of Interpretable Photoplethysmography Features for Blood Pressure Category Classification
paper_abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) provides waveform features for blood pressure (BP) category classification, but performance may vary across recording conditions. We evaluated a framework incorporating Step-Morphological Decomposition (SMD) on Aurora-BP, PPG-BP, PulseDB-Vital and the Synchronized Signals from Wearable Cardiovascular Monitoring Sensors dataset (SWCS). Signals were processed at 125 Hz. Conventional and neural classifiers were compared using subject-grouped evaluation, feature-family ablation, Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and cross-cohort adaptation. On Aurora-BP, XGBoost achieved a mean three-class macro one-versus-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.778 ± 0.011 across five folds. Subject-aggregated binary prediction achieved AUC 0.841. Source-only AUCs were 0.662 ± 0.096 on PPG-BP, 0.556 ± 0.049 on PulseDB-Vital and 0.696 ± 0.083 on SWCS. A restricted PPG-only pipeline achieved AUC 0.704. Removing the SMD feature family changed AUC from 0.778 to 0.776. Period morphology had the largest summed SHAP attribution, whereas demographic predictors had the largest average attribution per feature. Adaptation effects varied across cohorts and available target data. These retrospective results characterize the performance and limitations of the evaluated feature framework. Prospective clinical screening performance was not evaluated.

paper_title: Chart Reasoning with Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_abstract: Chart reasoning requires multimodal models to interpret visual encodings, derive structured semantics, execute formal reasoning procedures, and generate evidence-grounded outputs. This survey reviews chart reasoning methodologies for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), categorizing them by their primary intervention points: data and supervision design, inference-time reasoning strategies, and model-integrated optimization. We examine how existing approaches extract chart semantics, use intermediate representations, execute reasoning workflows, ground predictions in visual evidence, and verify outputs. We also summarize major chart reasoning benchmarks and cross-paradigm empirical results, and examine limitations in current evaluation protocols and metrics. Finally, we discuss recurring challenges in synthetic-to-real generalization, semantic reconstruction, visual grounding, reasoning faithfulness, and diagnostic evaluation, outlining directions toward more reliable and generalizable chart reasoning systems.

paper_title: Two Kinds of Inconsistency: A Constructive Note on the Empirical and Analytical Evaluation of the Energy Balance Model
paper_abstract: Arencibia-Albite presents two arguments against the Energy Balance Model: numerical tests showing that its predictions diverge from measurement, and an analytical proof showing that it is internally inconsistent when obligatory nitrogen loss is accounted for. These arguments are frequently treated as a single case. They are not. They describe two different kinds of failure, with different causes and different corrections. The analytical argument has been addressed elsewhere: when the chemical enthalpy carried out of the body by unoxidized nitrogen is included in the energy balance equation, the contradiction resolves – and the corrected model requires a mass-based term. The numerical argument is weakened by methodological asymmetries that can inflate the apparent empirical failure of the model. Absorption corrections applied asymmetrically across trial phases, and extrapolation from weekly chamber measurements to 14-day ward expenditure, can shift the calculated energy balance systematically. These asymmetries do not refute Arencibia-Albite's conclusion. They refine its evidential basis. When both arguments are corrected, what remains is a mass-based framework. This is not a critique of his work. It is its logical continuation.

paper_title: Tailored Induction for International Medical Graduates: Development and Evaluation of a Structured Onboarding Program at a UK Teaching Hospital
paper_abstract: International medical graduates (IMGs) constitute an increasing proportion of the UK medical workforce but often encounter professional, cultural, and practical challenges when transitioning into the NHS. At University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust (UHB), IMGs account for up to 75% of newly appointed locally employed doctors. In response to national guidance, UHB developed a tailored induction and onboarding program comprising a two-day, face-to-face course aligned with the four nationally defined induction domains. Delivered bimonthly by a multidisciplinary faculty, the program integrates interactive teaching, practical clinical skills training, simulated communication exercises, pre-arrival resources, peer support, digital learning materials, and a structured four-week integration period. Program evaluation included standardized quantitative and qualitative feedback from 213 participants across 14 induction cycles between May 2023 and July 2024. Mean satisfaction scores exceeded 4.5/5 for all sessions, with clinical skills and e-portfolio/appraisal sessions receiving the highest ratings (4.81/5). Participants reported improved confidence in clinical procedures, greater understanding of NHS systems, and increased confidence in career development. Feedback identified opportunities to expand IT systems training and optimize session scheduling. A structured, IMG-specific induction program can support successful transition into NHS practice, enhance preparedness for clinical work, and provide a scalable model for organizations recruiting international doctors.

paper_title: Decision Models as Product Rerankers for E-Business Search and Recommendation: An Independent Evaluation on the Amazon Shopping Queries Dataset
paper_abstract: Which products a shopper sees first, in search results or recommendations, shapes what they buy. Retailers increasingly use language models to judge product relevance. Decision models (Jev, Clef and Perplexity Decider) return a probability for each permitted judgement instead of generated text, which makes them natural rerankers for search and recommendation. We present, to our knowledge, the first independent, pre-specified evaluation of decision models on the Amazon Shopping Queries (ESCI) benchmark, with 1,000 US-English, 200 Spanish and 200 Japanese queries. Baselines were a dedicated reranker (Qwen3-Reranker-4B), general-purpose language models, a cross-encoder fine-tuned on 50,000 in-domain pairs, and BM25. Every decision model improved nDCG@10 over BM25, by 0.084 to 0.114 in English and by 0.100 to 0.149 in Spanish and Japanese (for Japanese, against a BM25 with character-bigram segmentation). Perplexity Decider ranked best (0.822) and significantly outperformed the dedicated reranker (0.787) by 0.032 to 0.035, whether run locally or through its hosted API. Asking for a four-way relevance label, an ordinal score or a yes/no exact-match judgement mattered little; the four-way label was best or tied in every comparison. All systems confused Exact with Substitute products; recall of Complement products, which underpin accessory recommendations, ranged from 15% to 68%. Clef’s labels were unaffected by the order of answer options, which it sorts internally, whereas a general-purpose language model changed up to 26% of its labels. The hosted Perplexity API reranked 1,000 queries for US$0.10–0.14 and, with the yes/no design, lay on the cost–quality frontier. We discuss implications for retailers, marketplaces, recommender systems and shopping agents.

paper_title: Fuzzy Evaluation of Glycemic Load and Beta-Glucan Intake: Deriving a Type 2 Diabetes–Preventive Dietary Circle
paper_abstract: Background/Objectives: Diabetes mellitus type 2 (T2D) is a global epidemic affecting over 500 million adults. Glycemic load (GL) and beta-glucan intake are modifiable dietary risk factors for T2D that are largely shaped by the choice of cereal-based foods. This study derives fuzzy sets for GL and beta-glucan to enable joint nutritional evaluation within a multidimensional framework and uses the framework to generate a T2D-preventive dietary circle. Methods: Fuzzy membership functions for GL and beta-glucan were constructed based on epidemiological dose–response data and established dietary reference values. These functions were integrated into the existing Nutritional Value Score (NVS II) system, which aggregates the evaluation of nutrient intake using a Schweizer–Sklar T-norm (p = 6). A fuzzy optimization algorithm was applied to an average representative German omnivore diet to derive a T2D-preventive dietary circle. Results: The GL fuzzy set reaches its optimum at ≤80 g/d and penalizes intakes ≥160 g/d; the beta-glucan fuzzy set reaches its optimum at ≥3 g/d. Fuzzy optimization shifted the diet markedly toward vegetables, legumes, fish, and tofu while strongly reducing cereals and milk products. The resulting dietary circle achieved an evaluation > 0.9 for the intake of every nutrient and an aggregate score of 0.894. Conclusions: Integrating GL and beta-glucan into the fuzzy evaluation framework yields a coherent, food-based T2D-preventive dietary circle that can serve as a practical reference for counseling, menu planning and intervention studies.

paper_title: Design and Evaluation of PPO-Based Coordinated P–Q Control for a Smart-Inverter BESS in PV–EV Distribution Networks
paper_abstract: Phase-asymmetric electric-vehicle (EV) charging can aggravate voltage unbalance in radial distribution feeders, while a smart-inverter battery energy storage system (BESS) can provide both energy shifting and fast reactive-power support. This study designs and evaluates a proximal policy optimization (PPO)-based controller for coordinated active- and reactive-power dispatch under asymmetric EV demand. The analysis uses a corrected phase-decoupled three-phase extension of the IEEE 33-bus feeder, with voltage unbalance quantified using the negative-to-positive sequence voltage ratio. Active-power-only (P-only) and coordinated P–Q controllers are evaluated using identical BESS hardware, operating limits, and terminal state-of-charge (SOC) requirements, enabling the incremental contribution of inverter reactive-power capability to be assessed under matched conditions. Across three independent training seeds, P–Q control reduces daily feeder loss from 3874.822 to 3809.751 kWh/day, worst voltage-unbalance factor (VUF) from 2.7879% to 2.5940%, and mean hourly maximum VUF from 1.5422% to 1.3628%, corresponding to reductions of 1.679%, 6.954%, and 11.632%, respectively, relative to the no-BESS case. The corresponding P-only reductions are 0.610%, 4.362%, and 8.427%, respectively. All reported learned-policy evaluations return the BESS to 50% terminal SOC, preventing the comparison from being biased by net battery depletion. Without retraining, the P–Q policies retain approximately 5.66–7.86% mean worst-VUF reduction under the tested load, photovoltaic, EV-demand, and combined-profile perturbations. The results demonstrate repeatable voltage-unbalance mitigation and show that coordinated P–Q operation provides an incremental benefit beyond active-power-only control under the investigated conditions. However, residual undervoltage under severe loading and the phase-decoupled feeder representation limit the scope of the conclusions.

paper_title: Evaluation of Ozonated Water’s Efficacy in Rinsing Equipment in a Processed Fishery Products Industry
paper_abstract: Ozonated water may represent a complementary approach to improve routine hygiene during fish processing. This study evaluated its effectiveness in reducing microbial contamination on food-contact surfaces of a cod-processing machine during scheduled production breaks and at the end of production. Tap water and ozonated water were compared under routine industrial conditions by monitoring Total Mesophilic Counts (TMC) and Total Psychrotrophic Counts (TPC) at multiple time points throughout the working day. Both treatments reduced microbial loads, but ozonated water achieved significantly greater reductions in TMC and TPC during morning and end-of-day rinsing, whereas no significant difference was observed during the lunch rinse. Microbial loads increased again during subsequent processing periods under both treatments. After final chlorine-based sanitation, TMC remained significantly higher in the ozonated water treatment, while no difference was observed for TPC. Overall, ozonated water improved the effectiveness of selected rinsing procedures under real processing conditions and should be considered complementary to conventional end-of-day cleaning and disinfection. Its use during production breaks may therefore represent a practical complementary measure for controlling microbial accumulation in fish processing environments.

paper_title: SteelWire Rope Degradation and Non-Destructive Characterization: Physical Mechanisms, Standards, and Intelligent Assessment
paper_abstract: Steel wire ropes are load-bearing components of hoisting, traction and cable systems whose degradation is concealed and cumulative, so their inspection is safety-critical. This review treats wire-rope non-destructive testing (NDT) as a materials problem, since what is measured is the state of the steel, and asks how physical sensing mechanisms, quantitative damage characterisation, data reliability and engineering standards can be integrated into one framework on which a discard decision can rest. First, degradation is mapped onto the observables that detect it through three inspection axes: the loss of metallic cross-sectional area (LMA) for distributed degradation, local flaws (LF) for broken wires, pits and cracks, and the mechanical state for damage that is neither, such as residual stress and fatigue damage. Second, three analytical results are derived and reported with their limits: a saturating magnetic-flux-leakage amplitude law for which amplitude-only depth inversion becomes severely ill-conditioned, an eddy-current skin depth that confines conventional excitation to the near surface, and a nearly non-dispersive fundamental longitudinal mode in an idealised single steel wire below 500 kHz·mm. Third, a protocol audit shows that published deep-learning figures are not comparable, and a unified evaluation protocol is proposed.

paper_title: Structure-Based Drug–Drug Interaction Prediction from Morgan Fingerprints: A Degree-Controlled and Cold-Start Evaluation of a Random Forest Baseline
paper_abstract: Drug–drug interaction (DDI) checkers can only look up combinations that have already been recorded, so they say nothing about pairs that were never studied together, such as those involving newly approved drugs. We ask how much of the apparent performance of a structure-only DDI model survives a careful evaluation. Each drug is represented by Morgan (ECFP) fingerprints and ten physicochemical descriptors computed from PubChem SMILES (1,688 of 1,701 drugs in a DrugBank-derived list resolved), and a drug pair by order-invariant combinations of the two drugs’ features. We first show that a common negative sampling protocol, which screens random negatives only against the sampled positives, labels 20.9 ± 0.8% of its “non-interacting” pairs with recorded interactions. We then build two balanced benchmarks of 17,522 pairs whose negatives exclude every recorded pair: one with random negatives and one with degree-matched negatives. On the random-negative benchmark a control that uses only drug identity, with no chemistry, reaches ROC-AUC 0.758, comparable to Random Forests on fingerprints (0.753–0.768). On the degree-matched benchmark the control falls to or below chance, the original concatenated-fingerprint model drops to AUC 0.572, and the order-invariant feature set with descriptors reaches AUC 0.678 (accuracy 62.1%) on random pairs and 0.615 (accuracy 57.6%) when both drugs are unseen in training. Calibration, selective prediction and a ten-pair case panel show that the model misses many recorded interactions (for example Sildenafil + Nitroglycerin) and is best used with an explicit “uncertain” output, which a Streamlit prototype provides. This work is a research prototype and is not intended for clinical use.

paper_title: AI-Enabled Security Benchmarks for FR3 Ultra-Massive MIMO 6G IoT Networks: Network Intrusion Detection and Angle-of-Arrival Spoofing Detection
paper_abstract: This paper presents two related benchmark studies of AI-enabled security for FR3 (7-24 GHz) ultra-massive MIMO (UM-MIMO) 6G IoT networks, addressing two different layers of the security stack. Study 1 evaluates machine learning approaches for network-layer intrusion detection using a telecom-relevant benchmark dataset (UNSW-NB15), cross-validating multiple classifiers and reporting a systematic literature synthesis, data-quality audit, and hyperparameter-tuned test-set performance comparison. Study 2 evaluates physical-layer angle-of-arrival (AoA) spoofing detection for FR3 UM-MIMO IoT authentication, benchmarking equal and adaptive snapshot-allocation policies for multi-device authentication under a shared sensing budget, validated against closed-form Cramer-Rao bound theory. Together, the two studies show that AI-enabled security benchmarking must be evaluated separately at each layer, network-layer intrusion detection depends primarily on model choice, hyperparameter tuning, and data-quality awareness, while physical-layer spoofing detection depends primarily on how a shared sensing budget is allocated across devices, indicating that a defence-in-depth FR3 UM-MIMO IoT security posture needs distinct, layer-appropriate AI benchmarking rather than a single unified approach.

paper_title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
paper_abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

paper_title: Can It Actually Work? Synthesizing Functional CAD Mechanisms
paper_abstract: While LLM agents can generate visually plausible CAD assemblies, these designs often fail to fulfill their intended physical functions. We study functional CAD design, a setting where agents interpret underspecified requests to construct and iteratively revise mechanisms that satisfy functional requirements in physical simulation. Verifying these requirements is nontrivial: different candidate mechanisms may realize the same function through entirely different components, controls, and operating sequences. To bridge this gap, we propose FunCAD-Harness, a framework that translates abstract requirements into candidate-specific physical tests and uses simulation feedback to guide design revisions. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce FunCADBench, a benchmark spanning 46 mechanism families with interdependent and multi-step operations. Experiments across frontier LLM agents show that FunCAD-Harness exposes subtle mechanical failures invisible to visual inspection, substantially improving functional success rates over standard simulation-augmented baselines. Ultimately, our work marks a step toward CAD agents capable of translating human intent into working mechanisms.

paper_title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
paper_abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.

paper_title: VideoMaMa++: Temporally Consistent Video Matting via Preserve-and-Refine Token
paper_abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.

paper_title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
paper_abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $Ψ_0$, $ω$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.

paper_title: GenOlympiad: Benchmarking Frontier Image Models at Their Capability Boundaries
paper_abstract: Text-to-image models have made tremendous progress and can produce high-quality images. However, a question which would be asked in any other discipline is where the frontier models fall short. We introduce GenOlympiad, a benchmark which provides the most challenging text prompts from nine capability axes for stress-testing frontier text-to-image models. The assessed capabilities include generating large quantities, performing deep reasoning, ensuring hard physical consistency, following complex rules and so on. The prompts are designed such that prompt alignment is visually verifiable (e.g., counting) instead of relying on subjectiveness (e.g., style). Based on this, we develop an automated evaluation framework which decomposes the prompt into easy and hard questions, and for most hard questions, draws help lines to ground evidence for accurate grading. We evaluate 20+ strong text-to-image models, including Nano Banana Pro, GPT-Image-2.5, Seedream-5.0 and so on. We report that even the best-performing T2I model (Nano Banana Pro) only achieves a strict score of 23.9 out of 100 and that coding models such as GPT-6 Astra have higher prompt alignment scores (but not as visually pleasing). We also derive insights in model evolution, alignment with Elo scores, and effectiveness of our grounding-based evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/GenOlympiad/GenOlympiad and the project page is at https://genolympiad.github.io/

paper_title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
paper_abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.

paper_title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
paper_abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.
comments: 24 pages, 14 figures, 12 tables, including references and appendices

paper_title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
paper_abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

paper_title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
paper_abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.

paper_title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
paper_abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.

paper_title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
paper_abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.
comments: 24 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Benchmark and tasks: https://github.com/Protege-AI/ProteinGeoBench

paper_title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
paper_abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.

paper_title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
paper_abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.

paper_title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages
paper_abstract: Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.
comments: accepted at 2026 IEEE Spoken language Technology Workshop Demo Track

paper_title: State World Models: Execute the Rules, Generate the Pixels
paper_abstract: Existing world models can generate action-conditioned video from a single image. Many focus on camera movement, allowing users to explore the generated scene. However, navigation alone does not ensure that an action follows persistent rules when its outcome depends on state that is invisible in the current frame. We present Stateful Harness, a framework that separates world evolution from video rendering to support stateful and rule-governed interaction. It maintains an evolving world state under specified rules, renders each resulting event with a frozen video model, and uses the generated clip to update the world state for the next turn. At each turn, the harness resolves the action selected by the user and compiles the resulting event into an instruction, while a preview clip from an editable 3D scene provides spatial and camera guidance. To evaluate rule compliance, we build WorldState-Bench, a benchmark of 50 counterfactual twin pairs that share an initial frame and action but differ in hidden state and required outcome. Under rule-only prompting, the best of the 11 evaluated video backends produces the required endings for both cases in 32% of pairs. For MiniMax-H3, specifying the required endings raises this rate from 32% to 64%, while the full harness reaches 92% with the same frozen model. These results support separating rule execution from video rendering for world interactions with hidden state.

paper_title: Learning to Refer: Inference-Time Collaboration in Decentralized Federated Learning
paper_abstract: In decentralized federated learning, heterogeneous clients may develop complementary expertise, yet each query is typically evaluated only by the client where it arrives. To exploit this distributed expertise without global coordination, we formulate inference-time collaboration as budgeted local expert referral, a graph-constrained routing process in which a query can move only between neighboring clients and only visited clients contribute to its final prediction. EdgeDRM implements this framework by learning a density-based routing potential for each client: differences between neighboring potentials provide the comparisons used to select successive referrals, while local task models generate predictions that are aggregated along the resulting route. Both training and inference are decentralized, using only neighbor-local information without a central router or graph-wide client scoring. We establish estimation guarantees for the learned comparisons and characterize how local improvement and graph structure govern prior-weighted density gains from referral. Experiments on benchmark and real-world medical data show that EdgeDRM outperforms graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, with the clearest benefits under sparse connectivity.

paper_title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
paper_abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.

paper_title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
paper_abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .
comments: Accepted at the 2026 Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD 2026)

paper_title: HarnessPro: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement with Pareto Optimization for Performance-Cost Trade-offs
paper_abstract: Harness development plays a crucial role in building capable AI agents. Recent approaches improve harnesses through recursive self-improvement (RSI), but their performance gains often come with higher execution costs. We introduce HarnessPro, a label-free method for evolving harnesses to improve task performance while reducing execution cost. In this setting, candidate harnesses are evaluated using LLM-generated tests without access to ground-truth solutions or official tests. Specialized agents diagnose execution trajectories, plan updates with different performance-cost priorities, and implement them as candidate harnesses. Rather than returning a single harness, HarnessPro uses normalized weighted squared-distance selection to provide cost-focused (lite), balanced (medium), and performance-focused (heavy) harnesses for different deployment budgets. Selected harnesses enter the next iteration, where execution feedback guides further updates. Our experiments cover Terminal-Bench 2, SWE-Bench Pro, and ProgramBench, using GPT-5.5 with Codex and GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Across these benchmarks using GPT-5.5 with Codex, the heavy mode of HarnessPro achieves an average pass-rate gain of 2.0 percentage points and an average per-task cost reduction of 26.1% relative to RHO. This advantage also holds when using GLM-5.2 with Claude Code. Code is available at https://github.com/pzs19/HarnessPro

paper_title: Beyond Omni: A Unified MLLM for Embodied Sensory Understanding
paper_abstract: Recent embodied systems increasingly build on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for their pretrained understanding and reasoning capabilities, but their perception of the physical world remains largely limited to basic modalities such as vision and audio. However, broadening MLLMs to more diverse sensory modalities from the physical environment is challenging: their representations are often weakly connected to the MLLM and vary substantially in structure and statistics, while their interpretation still requires shared high-level understanding and reasoning. We therefore propose Unisense, a unified embodied MLLM framework that supports diverse physical sensory modalities within a shared multimodal architecture. Unisense follows a two-stage training process: (i) aligning sensory representations with language to establish a language-accessible interface; and (ii) tuning modality-specific experts within the shared LLM to provide specialized processing for different sensory modalities. To support broad sensory learning, we curate Unisense-1M, a large-scale embodied sensory training corpus comprising 1M samples across 8 sensory modalities. We further evaluate Unisense on 12 benchmarks spanning depth, point cloud, IMU, tactile, thermal, radar, motion, and smell understanding. Across these heterogeneous sensing tasks, Unisense achieves strong performance and outperforms both generalist and specialized models on most benchmarks, demonstrating the potential of pretrained MLLMs as unified models for embodied sensory understanding.

paper_title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation
paper_abstract: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. Such labels are cheap to collect from crowdworkers or vision-language models (VLMs), making them attractive for large-scale annotation. However, both sources can mistakenly assign the true class as the complementary label. Such annotation errors are particularly harmful in CLL because the model is explicitly trained to suppress the correct answer. Optimal transport (OT) data valuation identifies harmful samples by comparing training data with a clean validation set, but transferring it directly to CLL creates a semantic mismatch: label $c$ means not class $c$ in the training but class $c$ in the validation. We show that this makes the OT label groups noisy mixtures whose behavior depends on the noise rate. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. The margin keeps a consistent direction across noise rates, detects diagonal noise with a parameter-free threshold of closed-form precision, and allows detected samples to be recycled as ordinary-label supervision. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. With only a fraction of the clean validation data, it also improves every CLL objective we evaluate, showing that OT-based valuation becomes reliable once the semantics of complementary supervision are modeled explicitly.

paper_title: PVBench: Quantifying Physical Plausibility in Video Generation with Object-Level Physical Measurements
paper_abstract: Recent video generation models produce visually compelling outputs, yet their physical plausibility remains poorly measured. Physical plausibility asks whether generated objects obey geometry, kinematics, dynamics, and conservation laws. Existing benchmarks rely on coarse visual-language model judgments or target embodied world models rather than video generation itself. We introduce PVBench, a physical video benchmark that quantitatively measures the plausibility of generated videos across 46 dimensions organized into seven domains, spanning: i) instruction and semantic fidelity, ii) behavioral and causal consistency, iii) perceptual and temporal quality, iv) geometric and spatial consistency, v) material properties and field states, vi) kinematic and spatiotemporal persistence, vii) and mechanical plausibility with conservation laws. PVBench comprises 600 carefully crafted prompts, of which 30% involve physical embodied agents such as robot arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and multi-agent systems. For challenging physically tractable dimensions, it pairs each with specialized vision models that derive verifiable, physically grounded measurements, such as object-level 6D pose, metric scale, surface normals, kinematics, and numerical conservation-law residuals. It thus avoids relying solely on subjective scoring, while supporting both text-to-video and image-to-video generation. Finally, we validate the agreement between automatic metrics and human judgments through human evaluation. Meanwhile, we evaluate mainstream open-source and closed-source models and present several insights. By releasing the benchmark, prompts, and calibration protocol, we aim to foster physically grounded video generation.

paper_title: Parallel Language Models via Variational Decoding
paper_abstract: Autoregressive language models emit one token per forward pass. This causes high inference latency, in particular as models are scaled up for quality. In this paper, we introduce Parallel Language Models (PLMs), which generate mutually consistent tokens in one forward pass by routing dependencies through latent auxiliary variables. PLMs are trained using a variational bound that reduces to an autoregressive loss plus a parallel decoding loss. Empirically, PLMs are on a faster and better Pareto frontier than autoregressive and discrete diffusion baselines. Pretrained PLMs achieve near-autoregressive pretraining loss on model scales of 80M to 3B parameters, and speedup follows a power law in model size. When post-trained, our 1.3B model matches or exceeds an identically trained autoregressive model on math, coding, and instruction-following benchmarks, speeding up inference $2.3\text{-}5.7\times$. Together, we show that parallel generation can be trained from a single training objective at autoregressive quality. We will make our code available at https://github.com/mandt-lab/plm.

paper_title: BrushOff: Stroke-Based Re-rendering as a Watermark Removal Attack on Painting
paper_abstract: Invisible watermarks are used to mark who owns a painting. We show that a simple attack removes the most robust one we test. The attack redraws the watermarked painting with brush strokes, using a pretrained stroke-based renderer. We call this attack BrushOff. It needs no training, no knowledge of the watermark, and no generative model. We test four watermarks on 500 paintings from five styles. VINE, a recent watermark built to survive image editing, survives all 14 conventional distortions we test, with at least 97.8% detection. Repainting lowers its detection to 1.8%, while the output keeps a no-reference quality score close to that of the clean paintings. Diffusion regeneration can also remove VINE, but at the same removal level it moves the image twice as far from the painting in DreamSim distance, and it changes what the painting shows. Because the renderer draws a countable number of strokes, we can control the attack strength step by step. Finally, we test what kind of signal survives. A simple probe that stores bits in the relative brightness of neighboring regions survives repainting, while a probe that uses absolute brightness does not. The same probe fails under diffusion regeneration, while VINE fails under repainting. Robustness to these two attacks is therefore a separate property, and benchmarks should test both.

paper_title: StepBench: Diagnosing Real-World Procedural Understanding in AI Agents
paper_abstract: Evaluating an agent's planning ability remains challenging for open-domain tasks, where verifying procedures through execution is often impractical. Existing evaluations typically assess only the final plan and do not distinguish procedural errors such as missing, incorrect, or misordered actions. We introduce STEPBENCH, a benchmark of 6,885 verified procedures crawled from wikiHow across 81 open-domain categories. From each procedure, we derive 5 diagnostic tasks: four with deterministic answers involving withheld, incorrect, or shuffled steps, and one requiring next-step generation. We additionally evaluate full-plan generation to examine how diagnostic performance correlates with end-to-end plan validity. Using the same procedures across tasks lets us directly compare different planning capabilities. For generation, STEPEVAL identifies critical failures that prevent goal completion. Across 14 configurations of 12 models, we find substantial differences across planning capabilities, with step ordering proving the most difficult: the strongest model correctly orders only 63.0% of procedures, dropping to 33.1% for those with nine or more steps. Incorrect-step detection also predicts judged plan validity across models, suggesting a lower-cost alternative for evaluating generation quality. On STEPBENCH-Val, comprising 214 procedures published in 2026, comprehension scores and rankings remain stable, suggesting limited influence from memorisation.

paper_title: Which Model for Which Role? Cost-Efficient Pareto Recommendation for LLM Agentic Workflows
paper_abstract: LLM agentic workflows increasingly employ different models for specialized roles. Users may prefer different trade-offs between task quality and deployment cost, sometimes also considering latency. Finding good assignments incurs a separate search cost from evaluating multiple candidates. We introduce Cost-Coupled Gittins (CC-Gittins), a multi-objective extension of single-objective cost-aware Gittins search for Pareto recommendation. It exploits the coupling between evaluation and deployment costs: assignments that cost more to deploy also cost more to evaluate. The search alternates between seeking higher quality and lower deployment cost, reusing each evaluation to inform both searches. After each batch, CC-Gittins recommends assignments that are nondominated under uncertainty-adjusted estimates of quality and deployment cost. We evaluate CC-Gittins on eight quality--cost matrices from workflows with two to five roles and up to 1,681 candidate assignments. We also evaluate the method with latency as a third objective. Across the eight benchmarks, CC-Gittins recovers a substantial fraction of the true Pareto frontier at roughly 10% of the exhaustive-evaluation cost, and recovers most of the frontier with few false positives by 30%.
comments: Preliminary version accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Resource-Aware Agentic AI (RAAAI)

paper_title: AllPath: Layered Verification for a Deployed, Self-Revising LLM Trading Agent under Human-Gated and Autonomous Regimes
paper_abstract: LLM trading agents are evaluated almost exclusively in backtests and autonomous benchmark harnesses. Deployment, where actions are irreversible, raises a different question: who verifies the agent's actions, and which failures can each verifier structurally catch? We report on AllPath, a personal LLM trading agent deployed against a live paper-brokerage account. The system watches positions through a deterministic rules engine, and each night it reviews its own day and proposes revisions to its own trading strategies. Verification is split across three layers. Code verifies what must not depend on judgment: deterministic gates enforce risk limits and block any strategy revision that fails an integrity check. The agent verifies itself within fixed bounds: its nightly review has an iteration cap and no tools that can act. A human verifies judgment, through approval screens that show the current state of each proposal. We also compared two verification policies for the agent's self-revisions on the live system: two and a half weeks with every self-revision human-gated, then five weeks with reflection revisions auto-applied behind the same code gates, while the operator's chat channel stayed human-gated throughout. Each layer caught a different kind of failure. The code gates rejected no proposal; their role was keeping revisions consistent. The human rejected two proposals that passed every code check, both over a disagreement about the market, and later removed 11 of the 19 rules the agent had added on its own, at a median lag of eight days. The most instructive production incidents, such as strategies silently left unmonitored, passed every gate; the operator found them by hand, and the fix each time was an interface change that makes the condition visible. We contribute the layered architecture, the two-regime account, and a production incident taxonomy, none observable in a backtest.
comments: Accepted to the 3rd Workshop on LLMs and Generative AI in Finance (AI4F) at ACM ICAIF 2026 (non-archival). 11 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://github.com/dukesky/allpath-trading-agent

paper_title: SpatialScout: Can VLM Agents Actively Explore and Map 3D Scenes?
paper_abstract: Spatial intelligence requires agents to actively acquire visual evidence and integrate observations into a coherent representation of the three-dimensional world. Yet spatial question answering offers limited evidence of whether models can construct accurate metric maps through autonomous exploration. We introduce SpatialScout, a benchmark for evaluating vision-language model (VLM) agents on active object-level 3D mapping. SpatialScout comprises 80 diverse indoor scenes containing 3,140 target objects. Given an object inventory, RGB observations, camera calibration, and camera poses, agents control a camera to explore each scene and estimate object centers in a shared coordinate frame. The task requires coordinating viewpoint selection, cross-view association, geometric estimation, and map revision under bounded interaction budgets. Evaluation jointly measures localization accuracy and target coverage through object-scale overlap scores that penalize missing predictions. Experiments with frontier VLMs reveal substantial limitations: the strongest evaluated model, Claude Opus 5.5, achieves a mean overlap score of 41.71%, with 47.23% of targets exceeding an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 and only 3.25% exceeding 0.9. These results reveal a substantial gap between recovering coarse object layouts and constructing complete, precise metric maps. SpatialScout provides a quantitative testbed for developing agents that build reliable 3D spatial representations through active perception. Code is available at https://github.com/JesseZZZZZ/SpatialScout.

paper_title: From Outcomes to Components: A Counterfactual Evaluation Framework for LLM-Proposed Repairs
paper_abstract: An LLM-generated repair action specifies which records to change and by how much. A failed action may still contain a useful target set or numerical update, depending on how the two are paired. We evaluate this problem in traffic networks and databases, where aggregate observations obscure the records that need correction. We examine the pairings by executing each combination from the same initial state, using a reference action that restores the affected records. In 76 of 114 traffic actions, the gain from correcting both parts exceeds the sum of the gains from correcting each part alone. Six of these actions become worse after either correction alone, but improve when both parts are corrected. In database repair, replacing only the proposed update with the reference update worsens 17 of 108 model actions, all of which select unaffected records. We also test whether parts of two proposals can be reused. On held-out observations, selecting among the proposals and their recombined target-update pairs recovers 61.6% of the reference action's loss reduction, compared with 58.0% from selecting between the proposals alone.

paper_title: Reasoning-Aware Multicalibrated Reliability Predictors for Language Models
paper_abstract: As people increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) for information, model providers need to communicate meaningful estimates of whether individual responses are correct or, more generally, reliable. In the context of hallucinations, existing work uses multicalibration to make such reliability predictions meaningful across application-relevant groups, such as prompt topics. Topic groups alone, however, can conceal systematic errors: within the same topic and confidence level, responses with different chain-of-thought (CoT) properties may exhibit opposing errors that cancel on average. In this work, we introduce reasoning-aware multicalibration, a framework that supplements application-relevant topic groups with groups derived from observable properties of CoT traces. We highlight that, theoretically, groupings based on CoT are "internally important", i.e., groupings for which the multicalibration guarantee is not societally crucial as it is for high-risk topics, but whose inclusion in the multicalibration procedure could easily and significantly improve predictive accuracy of the final reliability predictor. Empirically, we apply our framework to hallucination prediction and unsafe-response detection across a variety of benchmarks, and find that adding CoT groups to topic-based calibration reduces Brier score in both tasks. Interestingly, we find that multicalibrating with respect to CoT groups alone (without any topic information) already improves calibration across topics, suggesting that the predictor's errors depend on how the model reasoned, rather than what it was asked about in the prompt.

paper_title: Dual-Scale Condition-Shift Editing for Robust Real-World Image Demoiréing
paper_abstract: Robust demoiréing of screen-recaptured images remains challenging: moiré varies in frequency, color, and spatial support across display-camera pairs and capture conditions. Dedicated restoration networks trained on finite paired data struggle with this diversity, especially when low-frequency color banding and high-frequency stripes co-occur. We present DemoiréEdit, a content-preserving editing framework that adapts the natural-image prior of a pretrained flow-matching editor to demoiréing. First, an endpoint-supervised training objective supplements velocity matching with pixel, perceptual, and frequency-domain restoration losses. Second, a dual-scale condition-shift strategy performs global correction at low resolution, then refines the image at full resolution by shifting the denoising condition from the first-stage output to the original input for detail recovery. We also introduce DailyMoiré130, a benchmark of challenging moiré in everyday screen photography, comprising 130 smartphone captures across diverse displays with low-frequency color banding, fine high-frequency stripes, and mixed-frequency interference. On the challenging DailyMoiré130 benchmark, our method achieves the lowest residual moiré area and receives 71.3% overall-quality preference in a blind Best-of-7 study with 31 participants. We also evaluate on paired FHDMi/UHDM, reducing residual moiré confidence by 47.1%/9.3% and increasing MUSIQ by 4.3%/2.0% over the best baseline for each metric.

paper_title: When the harness decides success: state that cannot be re-observed
paper_abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.
comments: 14 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Pre-registered; code, pre-registration and cost ledger at https://github.com/raimondasl/persistgym

paper_title: EgoXperience: Learning World-Grounded Egocentric Representations from Human Experience
